title: Noninvasive Brain Imaging and Stimulation in Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation: A Review

subsections.section_title: Neuroimaging Modalities for Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: fNIRS for Rehabilitation Monitoring in Naturalistic Motor Tasks
subsections.content:
Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) is particularly valuable for post-stroke rehabilitation assessment because it measures cortical oxy-/deoxyhemoglobin changes with portable, silent, and motion-tolerant hardware, enabling repeated bedside monitoring during ecologically valid tasks such as reaching, grasping, gait, and upper-limb training in seated or standing positions ref [1], ref [2], ref [5], ref [6]. Compared with fMRI or PET, its major advantage is not anatomical precision but the capacity to capture rehabilitation-related hemodynamics during naturalistic behavior and over longitudinal recovery windows ref [1], ref [2], ref [6].

In stroke rehabilitation studies, fNIRS has consistently detected task-related reorganization of motor networks during realistic therapy paradigms. Longitudinal monitoring early after stroke shows that paretic upper-extremity movements are initially associated with more bilateral sensorimotor recruitment, followed by a progressive shift toward ipsilesional lateralization as motor function improves ref [4]. During active rehabilitation, limb-linkage training elicits asymmetric motor-cortical activation with altered effective connectivity, including enhanced influences toward contralesional prefrontal regions, suggesting compensatory recruitment of cognitive-control resources during demanding motor practice ref [3]. Broader neurorehabilitation reviews similarly indicate that fNIRS can track cortical changes across upper-limb therapy, gait, balance, and motor learning, and may provide surrogate markers of recovery or treatment response ref [2], ref [5].

These strengths should be interpreted alongside important limitations. fNIRS is largely restricted to superficial cortex, is vulnerable to scalp hemodynamics, probe-placement variability, and motion artifacts, and often benefits from short-separation regression, physiological monitoring, and multimodal integration with EEG or MRI for better spatial and mechanistic interpretation ref [1], ref [5], ref [6]. Even so, its ability to follow patients repeatedly during unconstrained rehabilitation makes fNIRS one of the most practical neuroimaging tools for monitoring post-stroke motor recovery in real-world therapeutic contexts ref [2], ref [6].

subsections.section_title: Neuroimaging Modalities for Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: MEG Markers of Cortical Oscillations and Plasticity in Stroke Rehabilitation
subsections.content:
MEG offers a distinctive window on post-stroke motor plasticity because it measures cortical electrophysiology directly and is less affected than hemodynamic methods by neurovascular uncoupling. Reviews of the field emphasize its value for tracking recovery-related changes in oscillations, connectivity, and source-level network reorganization, particularly within sensorimotor and perilesional cortex ref [7]. In rehabilitation studies, movement-related beta and gamma rhythms have emerged as the most consistent MEG markers of altered cortical excitability and motor-system reorganization after stroke ref [11], ref [12].

A central finding is that impaired motor function is associated with abnormal modulation of beta activity. During affected-hand movement, stroke patients show reduced movement-related beta desynchronization in ipsilesional M1 compared with controls, and smaller beta suppression is linked to greater motor impairment, suggesting deficient task-related release from the resting sensorimotor state ref [12]. Longitudinal and intervention work further indicates that these oscillatory signatures are plastic: after intensive task-oriented therapy, post-movement beta synchronization decreases in bilateral precentral cortex and supplementary motor areas, while movement-onset gamma synchronization is reduced in affected M1, with both measures correlating with behavioral improvement ref [11].

Beyond overt movement, MEG also captures rehabilitation-relevant modulation during action observation and action-execution paradigms. In subacute stroke, observing and simultaneously executing normal hand actions produces stronger M1 beta suppression than observation alone or execution while viewing the affected hand, supporting the use of externally modeled actions to engage residual motor networks ref [9]. Resting-state MEG adds complementary information: spontaneous oscillations may shift during recovery, with enhanced temporo-parietal ~10 Hz activity in the affected hemisphere during follow-up, whereas abnormal low-frequency magnetic activity near 1 Hz localizes to perilesional cortex, is associated with larger lesions, and may persist in patients with poorer outcome ref [7]. Source-space analyses also demonstrate increased delta/theta and reduced beta power, together with lower multiscale entropy, in structurally spared perilesional tissue, indicating that MEG can delineate "functionally lesioned" cortex as a potential target for neuromodulation and individualized rehabilitation planning ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Neuroimaging Modalities for Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: EEG Signal Processing and Machine Learning for Post-Stroke Classification
subsections.content:
EEG-based post-stroke classification has increasingly shifted from hand-crafted quantitative EEG descriptors toward data-driven pipelines that combine spectral decomposition, dimensionality reduction, and supervised learning. A common rationale is that stroke-related slowing, hemispheric asymmetry, and altered sensorimotor rhythms are encoded in multichannel, nonstationary signals that are poorly captured by single summary indices alone. Accordingly, recent studies have used wavelet or Fourier transforms to derive band-limited representations and then trained machine-learning classifiers to separate stroke from control subjects or stratify post-stroke severity groups ref [16], ref [17], ref [7], ref [9].

In relatively classical pipelines, spectral power and relative power ratio features remain effective low-dimensional biomarkers. A k-NN model using relative power ratios from delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands differentiated acute ischemic stroke severity groups with 85% test accuracy, illustrating the continued utility of interpretable frequency-domain features ref [17]. Related FFT-based approaches coupled with convolutional neural networks achieved about 90% test accuracy for post-stroke EEG detection, suggesting that deep models can exploit frequency representations without extensive manual feature engineering ref [7]. Wavelet-based preprocessing may be especially advantageous because EEG is strongly nonstationary; in one study, wavelet features combined with CNN improved post-stroke identification performance over more conventional spectral handling ref [16].

More recent work has emphasized representation learning and channel/data reduction to address redundancy in multichannel EEG. A PCA-CNN framework using wavelet-derived delta, theta, alpha, and mu components reported 93.33% accuracy with 45 principal components, outperforming the same architecture without PCA and highlighting the importance of compact multivariate representations ref [9]. Deep belief networks trained on slow cortical potentials have also been explored for stroke-related brain activity classification, indicating that hierarchical models can capture latent structure beyond shallow classifiers ref [6]. Collectively, these studies suggest that future progress will depend less on any single classifier than on robust preprocessing, artifact control, dimensionality reduction, and validation on larger, clinically heterogeneous datasets ref [16], ref [6], ref [9].

subsections.section_title: Neuroimaging Modalities for Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: EEG for Stroke Detection, Prognosis, and Motor Recovery Assessment
subsections.content:
EEG provides a rapid, portable, and bedside-accessible readout of cortical dysfunction, making it attractive for acute stroke detection when conventional imaging is delayed or unavailable. Across ischemic conditions, characteristic slowing with increased delta/theta activity, attenuation of alpha/beta rhythms, and interhemispheric asymmetry track reductions in cerebral perfusion and metabolism, supporting the physiological basis of quantitative EEG (qEEG) markers for ischemia detection ref [18], ref [19], ref [20]. Dense-array and whole-brain modeling further suggest that multichannel EEG features can capture neurological deficit severity beyond traditional single-lead metrics, with delta and beta power showing strong associations with NIHSS in acute ischemic stroke ref [18].

Among qEEG biomarkers, the brain symmetry index family has been especially important for triage and prognosis. Both the original and revised BSI distinguish stroke-related hemispheric imbalance from healthy patterns and correlate with impairment severity and short-term outcome ref [23], ref [8]. Studies of acute ischemic stroke report that higher rBSI is associated with lower Barthel Index, higher modified Rankin Scale scores, and worse neurological status, supporting its use as an early prognostic indicator ref [23]. More broadly, qEEG measures such as DAR, DTABR, relative band-power ratios, spectral edge frequencies, and mean frequency have shown relationships with infarct burden, NIHSS, and functional outcome in acute and subacute stroke ref [19], ref [20].

Beyond prognosis, EEG is increasingly used for automated stroke classification. Conventional signal-processing pipelines using spectral power, DAR/DTABR, and BSI have been coupled with machine-learning models such as extreme learning machines to classify acute ischemic stroke severity, while more recent 1D-CNN approaches learn discriminative patterns directly from PSD representations and achieve high reported accuracy for normal, mild, moderate, and severe stroke categories ref [9], ref [10]. In rehabilitation contexts, qEEG also shows value for recovery assessment: in chronic stroke, elevated slow-to-fast power ratios predict poorer upper-limb gains after robot-assisted therapy, suggesting that baseline cortical slowing may index limited neuroplastic reserve ref [21]. Overall, EEG complements structural imaging by linking detection, prognosis, and recovery potential within a single scalable modality ref [18], ref [21], ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Neuroimaging Modalities for Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: fMRI of Motor Reorganization and Connectivity After Stroke
subsections.content:
fMRI has been central to characterizing post-stroke motor reorganization at both the regional activation and network levels. Task-based studies consistently show that movements of the paretic hand recruit a distributed bilateral motor system, but the pattern is strongly shaped by time since stroke and initial impairment. In the first days after stroke, longitudinal fMRI revealed that recovery-related increases can emerge in ipsilesional and contralesional M1, premotor cortex, and SMA, with contralesional recruitment being especially prominent in more severely impaired patients ref [25]. By contrast, patients with milder deficits often show activation patterns closer to healthy controls ref [25], and hemispheric activation balance in M1 remains tightly linked to motor deficit across longitudinal follow-up ref [11].

Resting-state fMRI extends these observations by quantifying spontaneous coupling without requiring overt task performance. Acute reductions in interhemispheric motor connectivity are detectable within 24–48 h and are associated with hemiparesis severity ref [30], while stronger acute motor-network connectivity predicts better outcome in ischemic stroke ref [9]. Longitudinal studies further indicate that connectivity between ipsilesional and contralesional M1 becomes most asymmetric around the first month and then partially normalizes with recovery, whereas early preservation of connectivity with contralesional thalamus, SMA, and middle frontal gyrus is associated with better 6-month motor improvement ref [31]. More recent acute-stage work also suggests that weakened interhemispheric coupling, particularly between ipsilesional M1 and contralesional PMd, independently predicts unfavorable outcome ref [9].

Beyond undirected connectivity, effective-connectivity analyses suggest that stroke alters the direction of information flow within motor-control circuits. Resting-state Granger-causality studies reported abnormal influences between bilateral M1 and premotor-parietal-cerebellar regions, with more severe hand dysfunction associated with weaker causal interactions involving contralesional cerebellum and superior parietal cortex ref [14]. fMRI has also been used prognostically in the hyperacute phase, although adding early task fMRI to initial impairment yields only modest incremental value in severely affected patients ref [26]. Intervention studies nonetheless show that rehabilitation can reshape activation balance: after constraint-induced movement therapy, improvement is accompanied by greater contralateral SM1 engagement and ipsilateral cerebellar recruitment ref [27]. Together, these findings position fMRI as a key tool for tracking motor-network reorganization, identifying prognostic connectivity markers, and stratifying patients for restorative therapies.

subsections.section_title: Multimodal Imaging and Neurophysiological Coupling Approaches
subsections.subsection_title: Multimodal Imaging in Stroke Rehabilitation and Neurofeedback
subsections.content:
Multimodal imaging has become particularly valuable in rehabilitation studies that seek to link behavioral gains with both electrophysiological and hemodynamic plasticity. In chronic stroke, concurrent EEG-fMRI during brain-computer interface (BCI) or robotic training has shown that upper-limb improvement can be accompanied by coordinated reorganization within motor networks rather than isolated changes in a single modality. For example, BCI-guided robot-hand training was associated with increased resting-state connectivity between ipsilesional M1 and contralesional BA6, while EEG-derived directed information flow from premotor/SMA regions to ipsilesional M1 showed parallel changes that correlated with Fugl-Meyer gains, supporting cross-modal convergence on interhemispheric motor network rebalancing ref [33]. Related robotic-hand work further showed that reduced EEG interhemispheric asymmetry and increased fMRI interhemispheric connectivity covaried with motor improvement, suggesting that multimodal markers may capture complementary aspects of recovery-related normalization ref [34].

Beyond passive observation of post-training effects, multimodal systems have also been used as active neurofeedback interventions. A pilot bimodal EEG-fMRI neurofeedback study proposed a multi-target motor imagery paradigm that progressively shifted training emphasis toward ipsilesional M1 while still leveraging SMA engagement, demonstrating the feasibility of combined feedback in chronic stroke ref [35]. Importantly, successful upregulation of ipsilesional motor areas and clinical improvement were observed mainly in patients with preserved corticospinal tract integrity, highlighting that multimodal neurofeedback efficacy is constrained by residual structural reserve ref [35]. This aligns with broader BCI-neurorehabilitation literature showing that connectivity changes after feedback-based therapy are associated with behavioral gains ref [33].

Taken together, these studies indicate that multimodal imaging in stroke rehabilitation serves two complementary roles: mechanistic readout and therapeutic guidance. As a readout, EEG contributes temporal sensitivity to oscillatory desynchronization, complexity, and directed coupling, whereas fMRI localizes reorganization across distributed motor regions ref [33], ref [34]. As guidance, bimodal neurofeedback may improve target specificity compared with unimodal approaches by jointly constraining where and when self-regulation occurs ref [35]. Although current evidence remains limited by small samples and heterogeneous lesions, these early studies support multimodal biomarkers as promising tools for stratifying patients, monitoring plasticity, and optimizing individualized neurofeedback-based motor rehabilitation ref [33], ref [34], ref [35].

subsections.section_title: Multimodal Imaging and Neurophysiological Coupling Approaches
subsections.subsection_title: Concurrent EEG-fMRI Coupling and Network Fusion
subsections.content:
Concurrent EEG-fMRI coupling is a central strategy for linking millisecond electrophysiology to slower hemodynamic network organization. Methodological reviews have emphasized that simultaneous acquisition is uniquely valuable because it preserves the same behavioral state while enabling EEG-informed fMRI and fMRI-informed EEG analyses, despite persistent challenges from gradient and ballistocardiographic artifacts and unresolved questions about optimal fusion pipelines ref [36], ref [5], ref [6]. In motor systems, this framework is particularly relevant to stroke rehabilitation because it can relate oscillatory biomarkers to distributed reorganization of pericentral and premotor circuits.

A key finding from simultaneous resting-state studies is that sensorimotor rhythms covary with BOLD activity in anatomically plausible motor regions. Pericentral BOLD fluctuations track spontaneous alpha- and beta-band SMR power, with partial spatial dissociation between more posterior alpha-linked and more anterior beta-linked sensorimotor territories ref [37]. Related work likewise showed that mu/SMR amplitude is coupled to BOLD activity across sensorimotor, cingulo-insular, and associated control regions, supporting the view that resting oscillations index network-level excitability rather than isolated local generators ref [7], ref [8]. Such observations are highly pertinent in stroke, where abnormal beta and mu dynamics may reflect altered neurovascular and corticocortical coupling within recovering motor networks.

Beyond pairwise coupling, recent fusion approaches move into network space. Multimodal functional network connectivity models extract EEG and fMRI components separately, estimate directed interactions within each modality, and then align networks across modalities to build an integrated graph of common and modality-specific functional systems ref [38]. Complementarily, fMRI functional networks can be used as empirical priors for EEG source imaging, improving source reconstruction and enabling selection of the fMRI networks most supported by the EEG data ref [39]. These network-fusion strategies are promising for stroke because they could dissociate preserved from compensatory circuits, identify modality-convergent motor subnetworks, and provide individualized targets for neurofeedback or stimulation-guided rehabilitation ref [38], ref [39].

subsections.section_title: Multimodal Imaging and Neurophysiological Coupling Approaches
subsections.subsection_title: EEG-fNIRS and Portable Multimodal Monitoring
subsections.content:
Concurrent EEG-fNIRS systems are increasingly attractive in stroke rehabilitation because they combine EEG’s millisecond-scale sensitivity to oscillatory dynamics with fNIRS-based access to cortical hemodynamics in a portable, movement-tolerant format suitable for bedside and therapy-room deployment ref [40], ref [5], ref [6]. Compared with fMRI-centered multimodal paradigms, this configuration is better aligned with repeated monitoring during naturalistic motor practice, including sitting, grasping, and gait-related tasks that are common in rehabilitation workflows ref [40], ref [7], ref [8].

Early stroke-specific feasibility work showed that simultaneous EEG-fNIRS can distinguish patients from healthy controls through complementary interhemispheric markers derived from EEG entropy and HbO lateralization during hand grasping, suggesting sensitivity to abnormal hemispheric balance after subcortical stroke ref [4]. Extending this concept, an exploratory longitudinal study used fNIRS-informed EEG source imaging during hand clenching and reported reduced ipsilesional somatosensory activity in stroke, while increases in ipsilesional premotor strength and interhemispheric M1 connectivity tracked 4-week motor improvement; moreover, baseline premotor and SMA-M1 measures showed potential for outcome prediction ref [42]. These findings support EEG-fNIRS not merely as parallel sensing, but as a coupled framework for estimating recovery-relevant excitability and network reorganization.

From a translational perspective, wearable integrated EEG-fNIRS platforms now enable more compact caps, synchronized acquisition, and improved ecological validity, which may facilitate longitudinal phenotyping, neurofeedback, and home-based rehabilitation monitoring ref [40], ref [9], ref [10]. Nevertheless, important constraints remain, including limited depth sensitivity of fNIRS, susceptibility to extracerebral and motion artifacts, heterogeneous optode-electrode layouts, and the need for larger validation cohorts and standardized multimodal biomarkers in stroke populations ref [40], ref [41], ref [42]. Overall, portable EEG-fNIRS appears especially promising where repeated assessment of cortical state during active rehabilitation is prioritized over whole-brain coverage.

subsections.section_title: Multimodal Imaging and Neurophysiological Coupling Approaches
subsections.subsection_title: Reviews and Broader Multimodal Neuropsychiatric Context
subsections.content:
Broader reviews of multimodal neuroimaging provide useful context for stroke rehabilitation because they clarify why no single modality can adequately capture post-stroke reorganization across structural damage, electrophysiological dynamics, and hemodynamic compensation. A comprehensive review of multimodal neuroimaging computing in neuropsychiatric disorders emphasizes that MRI, PET, EEG, and MEG offer complementary spatial, temporal, and mechanistic information, and that clinically meaningful integration depends on robust preprocessing, feature extraction, fusion, and machine-learning pipelines rather than simple side-by-side interpretation ref [43]. This systems perspective is directly relevant to stroke, where recovery unfolds across distributed sensorimotor and cognitive networks rather than isolated lesions.

Although much of the broader multimodal literature comes from epilepsy, schizophrenia, dementia, and other neuropsychiatric conditions, several recurring themes are transferable to post-stroke motor rehabilitation: multimodal fusion can improve biomarker sensitivity, distinguish latent network subtypes, and support individualized prognosis and therapy selection ref [43]. The same review also highlights a key translational lesson for rehabilitation studies: multimodal datasets are most informative when they are explicitly linked to clinical phenotypes and longitudinal trajectories, rather than treated as purely descriptive imaging collections ref [43].

A complementary review focused on transcranial electrical stimulation and EEG/fNIRS features across brain diseases further broadens the neurorehabilitation context by summarizing how stimulation parameters, electrophysiological markers, and hemodynamic responses can be jointly optimized for closed-loop intervention design ref [44]. For stroke research, this literature supports the emerging view that multimodal monitoring is not only diagnostic but interventional: EEG can index fast cortical-state changes, fNIRS can track portable vascular responses, and combined readouts may help titrate stimulation intensity, timing, and target selection during training ref [44]. Together, these broader reviews argue that future stroke rehabilitation platforms should move toward standardized multimodal biomarkers, cross-modal validation, and adaptive stimulation-imaging frameworks that are generalizable beyond any single disorder class ref [43], ref [44].

subsections.section_title: Multimodal Imaging and Neurophysiological Coupling Approaches
subsections.subsection_title: Corticomuscular Coherence and Sensorimotor Pathway Coupling
subsections.content:
Corticomuscular coherence (CMC) provides a direct electrophysiological window onto sensorimotor pathway integrity by quantifying frequency-specific coupling between cortical activity and muscle output. In stroke, beta-band CMC is typically reduced in the acute stage and then strengthens with recovery, consistent with progressive re-establishment or rerouting of effective corticospinal communication ref [46]. Longitudinal and cross-sectional studies further show that recovery is often accompanied not only by changes in CMC magnitude, but also by spatial redistribution of coherent sources beyond canonical contralateral M1, including bilateral and posterior sensorimotor territories ref [46], ref [47].

This topographic variability is particularly relevant in patients with persistent impairment. In severely affected chronic stroke with hand paralysis, intervention-related gains after brain-robot training were associated with increased beta-band CMC in distributed premotor regions, especially ipsilesional premotor cortex, suggesting that premotor-muscular coupling can serve as a compensatory substrate and a candidate therapeutic target ref [50]. Such findings complement earlier reports that contralesional or non-primary motor coherence is not merely epiphenomenal, but may support residual motor output in selected patients ref [47], ref [50].

Methodologically, classic coherence is limited because it is undirected and predominantly linear. Work on sensorimotor coupling has shown that both descending motor commands and ascending somatosensory feedback contribute to CMC, and that directed coherence yields more physiologically plausible transmission delays than standard phase-based estimates ref [9]. Broader frameworks further argue that stroke-relevant coupling should be characterized in terms of directionality and nonlinearity, since cross-frequency interactions and closed-loop sensory feedback are missed by conventional CMC ref [48]. Information-theoretic approaches such as transfer spectral entropy extend this logic by resolving band-limited directional interactions, refining beta sub-band and gamma-band asymmetries in EEG-EMG coupling that may be useful for post-stroke biomarker development ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Techniques and Mechanistic Basis
subsections.subsection_title: Overview of Noninvasive Brain Stimulation in Stroke Rehabilitation
subsections.content:
Noninvasive brain stimulation (NIBS) has emerged as an adjunct to conventional post-stroke rehabilitation by leveraging activity-dependent plasticity rather than directly repairing injured tissue. Its rationale is grounded in the observation that motor recovery is shaped not only by corticospinal tract integrity, but also by post-stroke reorganization within distributed motor networks and by an imbalance of interhemispheric inhibition, in which the contralesional hemisphere may excessively suppress the lesioned motor cortex ref [51], ref [52], ref [53]. Within this framework, NIBS seeks either to facilitate residual excitability in the ipsilesional motor system or to damp maladaptive hyperexcitability in homologous contralesional regions ref [51], ref [53].

The two dominant clinical modalities are repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), which induces frequency-dependent excitatory or inhibitory after-effects, and transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), which modulates membrane polarization in a polarity-dependent manner ref [51], ref [52]. Across stroke studies, these approaches have been applied most often to upper-limb paresis, typically targeting primary motor cortex in chronic or subacute stages, although acute-phase interventions have also been explored ref [53], ref [4]. Importantly, NIBS effects are not purely local: stimulation alters connectivity in premotor, supplementary motor, thalamic, and other remote regions, reinforcing the view that stroke rehabilitation should be understood at the network level rather than as a single-site intervention ref [52].

At the same time, the clinical literature remains heterogeneous. Systematic reviews indicate modest but generally positive motor effects, tempered by substantial variability in lesion location, chronicity, baseline impairment, stimulation parameters, sham design, concomitant therapy, and outcome measures ref [4], ref [51]. Evidence also suggests that response may differ between cortical and subcortical strokes and between acute and chronic phases, underscoring the need for patient stratification and protocol optimization ref [51], ref [53], ref [4]. Thus, NIBS is best viewed as a biologically plausible, relatively safe, and promising enhancer of rehabilitation, but not yet a uniformly standardized therapy.

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Techniques and Mechanistic Basis
subsections.subsection_title: Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation: Protocols, Efficacy, and Clinical Evidence
subsections.content:
rTMS is among the most extensively studied noninvasive stimulation modalities for post-stroke motor rehabilitation, with protocols largely derived from the interhemispheric competition framework. Two canonical approaches predominate: low-frequency stimulation (usually 1 Hz) over contralesional M1 to suppress maladaptive transcallosal inhibition, and high-frequency stimulation (typically 3–10 Hz, sometimes higher) over ipsilesional M1 to facilitate excitability and promote motor output ref [54], ref [55]. Focused reviews emphasize that stimulation intensity is usually scaled to resting motor threshold, treatment courses range from single-session paradigms to 5–10 daily sessions, and safety is generally acceptable when standard guidelines are followed ref [54], ref [55].

Clinical efficacy is encouraging but heterogeneous. Meta-analyses report modest overall benefits of rTMS on upper-limb motor outcomes, with somewhat stronger effects for hand function and dexterity, and a recurrent signal favoring contralesional low-frequency stimulation, particularly in subcortical stroke and earlier phases of recovery ref [59], ref [60]. However, the Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to support routine use, largely because of small samples, variable endpoints, and protocol inconsistency ref [9]. These caveats are echoed in broader evidence syntheses that note conflicting effects on activities of daily living and limited certainty for long-term disability reduction ref [54], ref [9].

Randomized trials help clarify mechanistic and clinical distinctions. In early stroke, both ipsilesional 10-Hz and contralesional 1-Hz stimulation improved Fugl-Meyer scores relative to sham, while producing opposite but theoretically coherent neurophysiological and fMRI changes in ipsilesional versus contralesional motor networks ref [57]. Sustained gains have also been reported after either 1-Hz or 5-Hz protocols in ischemic stroke ref [10]. Moreover, bilateral coupling of inhibitory contralesional and facilitatory ipsilesional stimulation may outperform single-mode stimulation, suggesting that sequential rebalancing and excitation could enhance recovery in selected patients ref [13]. Overall, current evidence supports rTMS as a promising adjunct rather than a standardized standalone therapy ref [54], ref [55], ref [9].

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Techniques and Mechanistic Basis
subsections.subsection_title: Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation: Mechanistic Basis and Therapeutic Application
subsections.content:
Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) delivers weak direct current, typically 1–2 mA through scalp electrodes, to bias neuronal membrane potentials and thereby modulate cortical excitability in a polarity-dependent manner. In motor cortex, anodal stimulation generally increases excitability whereas cathodal stimulation decreases it; importantly, after-effects can outlast the stimulation period and are linked not only to membrane polarization but also to NMDA-receptor-dependent plasticity, GABAergic disinhibition, and neuromodulatory influences relevant to motor learning and consolidation ref [6]. In stroke rehabilitation, this physiology is usually interpreted through the lens of post-stroke interhemispheric imbalance, with stimulation aimed at either facilitating the ipsilesional motor cortex, suppressing contralesional overinhibition, or engaging both hemispheres simultaneously ref [62], ref [12].

Therapeutically, tDCS is attractive because it is portable, inexpensive, easy to combine with task practice, and generally well tolerated under standard protocols, with adverse effects usually limited to transient tingling, itching, or mild headache ref [62], ref [6]. Electrode montage is a central determinant of efficacy: anodal ipsilesional, cathodal contralesional, and bihemispheric montages have each shown short-term gains in hand motor performance, whereas extracephalic reference placements appear less consistent in stroke cohorts ref [11]. Small mechanistic and proof-of-concept studies further suggest that pairing stimulation with occupational therapy, constraint-induced movement therapy, robotic training, or peripheral stimulation may amplify training-related plasticity, especially in chronic stroke and in patients with residual corticospinal reserve ref [12], ref [11].

Clinical evidence, however, remains mixed. Systematic reviews indicate that pooled effects on motor outcomes are modest and often nonsignificant when all protocols and patient groups are combined, but benefits become more apparent in chronic stroke and milder-to-moderate impairment, highlighting substantial dependence on lesion characteristics, chronicity, dose, and concurrent therapy ref [10], ref [62]. More recent overviews similarly emphasize heterogeneity in stimulation intensity, timing relative to practice, session number, and outcome measures as major barriers to translation ref [12]. Thus, current consensus positions tDCS not as a standalone restorative therapy, but as a plasticity-priming adjunct whose clinical value will likely depend on individualized montage selection and integration with structured motor rehabilitation ref [10], ref [6], ref [12].

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Techniques and Mechanistic Basis
subsections.subsection_title: Targeted Functional Applications and Multimodal Stimulation Approaches
subsections.content:
Beyond generic upper-limb protocols, recent work has emphasized function-specific stimulation strategies and combination paradigms designed to engage task-relevant networks during rehabilitation. For lower-limb recovery, tDCS has been examined as an adjunct to gait-oriented training, with a systematic review and meta-analysis suggesting modest benefits for mobility and lower-limb strength, while effects on walking speed, endurance, and balance remain less consistent, underscoring the importance of outcome selection and patient stratification ref [67]. Pilot studies combining tDCS with robot-assisted gait training or task-related locomotor therapy similarly indicate that stimulation may be most useful when paired with active, repetitive practice rather than delivered in isolation ref [4], ref [5].

A related development is multimodal or dual-mode stimulation, in which distinct NIBS approaches are combined to shape interhemispheric dynamics more precisely. In healthy participants, simultaneous high-frequency rTMS over one M1 with contralateral anodal tDCS enhanced motor-evoked potentials and dexterity more than sham conditions, supporting the idea that interhemispheric modulation and homeostatic plasticity can be exploited in a coordinated manner ref [68]. Although direct stroke evidence remains limited, this framework is mechanistically attractive for tailoring excitatory and inhibitory influences according to lesion side, recovery stage, and residual corticospinal integrity ref [6], ref [7].

Another targeted direction couples stimulation with behaviorally meaningful sensorimotor priming. In subacute stroke, combined low-frequency rTMS and action observation improved distal hand performance and grip strength within the active-treatment group, while remaining safe and feasible, suggesting that stimulation may amplify mirror-neuron and motor-learning processes during observation-based practice ref [69]. Comparable logic underpins combinations with task-oriented therapy, strengthening exercise, robotic training, or brain-computer/virtual-reality interfaces, which seek to align neuromodulation with Hebbian, context-dependent plasticity rather than relying on stimulation alone ref [8], ref [9], ref [10]. Overall, multimodal approaches appear promising, but their superiority over well-designed unimodal protocols has not yet been established consistently in adequately powered trials ref [11], ref [12].

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Techniques and Mechanistic Basis
subsections.subsection_title: Broader and Cross-Condition Perspectives on Brain Stimulation
subsections.content:
Although stroke rehabilitation has largely focused on motor cortex stimulation, broader experience from psychiatry, pain, and other neuropsychiatric disorders provides useful perspective on how noninvasive brain stimulation should be developed clinically. In major depressive disorder, rTMS has matured from an experimental intervention into an evidence-based therapy, with protocol refinement around stimulation frequency, intensity, coil design, and target localization illustrating the importance of standardization and mechanistic targeting rather than assuming a single universal protocol ref [70]. Similar lessons are relevant to stroke, where heterogeneity in lesion location, network disruption, and recovery stage likely underlies variable treatment response.

Cross-condition work also reinforces several translational principles. First, stimulation effects depend on distributed networks rather than the local cortical site alone; depression studies emphasize how functional connectivity and neuronavigated targeting can improve engagement of relevant circuits, a concept directly applicable to post-stroke sensorimotor network modulation ref [70]. Second, newer paradigms such as theta-burst stimulation highlight how treatment duration can be shortened without necessarily sacrificing efficacy, which is especially relevant for rehabilitation settings where session burden and resource constraints limit scalability ref [70]. Third, maintenance, retreatment, and dose-scheduling questions remain incompletely resolved across disorders, underscoring the need for stroke trials to move beyond short-term impairment outcomes toward durability and real-world participation endpoints ref [70].

Finally, cross-condition evidence argues for a more personalized and multimodal future. In depression, inter-individual variability has motivated interest in imaging-guided targeting, electrophysiological biomarkers, and combined TMS-EEG approaches to predict and monitor response ref [70]. For stroke, analogous strategies may help identify who benefits from excitatory, inhibitory, bilateral, or accelerated stimulation paradigms, and when stimulation should be paired with robotics, task practice, action observation, or brain-computer interfaces. Thus, the broader brain-stimulation literature does not provide direct motor-recovery evidence, but it offers an important roadmap for protocol optimization, biomarker-guided stratification, and implementation science in neurorehabilitation ref [70].

subsections.section_title: Integrated Imaging-Stimulation Strategies and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Multimodal Imaging-Guided Brain Stimulation
subsections.content:
Multimodal imaging-guided brain stimulation has become a central strategy for personalizing post-stroke neuromodulation. Rather than stimulating canonical motor targets uniformly, combined TMS/tDCS with fMRI, EEG, DTI, or MRS can identify residual network capacity, interhemispheric imbalance, and structural constraints that shape responsiveness to stimulation ref [71], ref [72]. In stroke, this approach is especially valuable because lesion location, corticospinal tract integrity, and callosal microstructure strongly influence whether ipsilesional facilitation, contralesional inhibition, or alternative higher-order targets are most appropriate ref [72].

Conceptually, neuroimaging extends stimulation from a focal intervention to a network-level perturbation assay. Concurrent or sequential TMS-fMRI, TMS-EEG, and PET studies show that noninvasive stimulation modulates distributed cortical-subcortical systems beyond the coil or electrode, enabling causal tests of effective connectivity and compensation mechanisms after stroke ref [71], ref [72]. Resting-state and task-based measures can therefore be used not only to localize targets, but also to verify whether stimulation normalizes maladaptive motor-network interactions or recruits supportive premotor-parietal pathways ref [71], ref [72].

EEG-guided stimulation is particularly attractive for rehabilitation because of its temporal resolution and portability. Simultaneous high-definition tDCS-EEG demonstrates that stimulation induces acute and persistent changes in broadband cortical synchronization, including altered event-related desynchronization/synchronization over sensorimotor regions, indicating that electrophysiological signatures can serve as mechanistic readouts of dose and polarity effects ref [73]. In parallel, multimodal frameworks integrating TMS with structural and functional imaging have been proposed to stratify patients and optimize protocol selection, supporting a shift from one-size-fits-all stimulation toward biomarker-informed, adaptive neuromodulation in post-stroke motor recovery ref [72].

subsections.section_title: Integrated Imaging-Stimulation Strategies and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Network Mapping and Closed-Loop Frameworks
subsections.content:
A key next step beyond region-of-interest targeting is to model post-stroke motor control as a distributed sensorimotor loop rather than a purely cortico-cortical system. In this context, network mapping increasingly incorporates directed interactions among cortical nodes, descending corticospinal output, and afferent muscular feedback, allowing stimulation effects to be interpreted at the level of whole-loop reconfiguration rather than local excitability alone. The recent closed-loop cortico-muscular-cortical network framework is particularly relevant because it integrates EEG-EEG, EEG-EMG, and EMG-EMG coupling into a directional graph model, showing that low-frequency rTMS can strengthen interhemispheric motor information exchange while reducing maladaptive cortex-muscle coupling during movement after stroke ref [2].

Methodologically, these frameworks build on advances in corticomuscular coherence, directionality analysis, and graph-theoretic network metrics. Prior work showed that corticomuscular coherence is disrupted after stroke and changes with recovery, with shifts in the spatial locus and strength of coupling reflecting reorganization of descending motor control ref [13], ref [16], ref [49]. Studies on ascending and descending pathway contributions, as well as nonlinear and directional sensorimotor coupling, further support the idea that effective rehabilitation models should distinguish efferent from afferent information flow rather than treating connectivity as symmetric ref [14], ref [71], ref [70]. Graph analyses of post-stroke motor networks likewise indicate that recovery is associated with dynamic reorganization of network topology, motivating stimulation strategies that are adapted to evolving network states ref [36], ref [37].

These developments naturally motivate closed-loop stimulation architectures in which network estimates are used to personalize targets, timing, and stimulation polarity/frequency, and in turn are updated by ongoing electrophysiological feedback. Simultaneous EEG-fMRI and multimodal fusion studies have shown that network states can be inferred across complementary spatial and temporal scales, while source-informed EEG frameworks help constrain functionally meaningful stimulation nodes ref [57], ref [29], ref [42], ref [60]. Looking forward, clinically viable closed-loop systems will likely combine wearable EEG/EMG sensing, causal network inference, and adaptive stimulation controllers to track state-dependent recovery trajectories and intervene when pathological interhemispheric or corticomuscular patterns re-emerge.

subsections.section_title: Integrated Imaging-Stimulation Strategies and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Rehabilitation Technologies Combining Stimulation and Assistive Training
subsections.content:
A growing rehabilitation trend is the tight coupling of noninvasive stimulation with assistive training platforms that increase repetition, task specificity, and feedback. In this context, functional electrical stimulation (FES), robotics, augmented or virtual reality, and noninvasive cortical stimulation are used not as isolated add-ons, but as components of an integrated motor-learning environment. Early examples include augmented reality-based, EMG-triggered FES for ankle training, which improved paretic muscle activation and strength beyond FES alone in chronic stroke, illustrating how enriched sensory feedback can potentiate stimulation-assisted practice ref [75].

Robotic systems provide a particularly attractive scaffold for such combinations because they standardize movement kinematics, quantify performance online, and can be synchronized with adaptive stimulation. Iterative learning control frameworks for robot-assisted upper-limb rehabilitation have shown that FES can be titrated across repeated reaching trials to provide only the assistance needed, thereby preserving voluntary effort while improving tracking accuracy and reducing impairment over treatment sessions ref [76]. Related clinical work combining robot-assisted arm therapy with transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) suggests that gains are not uniform across patients: in an exploratory study, bilateral tDCS added to robotic training did not produce a simple overall group advantage, but its effect was modified by stroke duration and lesion type, with more favorable responses in chronic and subcortical stroke ref [77].

These findings support a shift from device-centric to patient-tailored rehabilitation technologies. Future systems will likely combine assistive robotics, peripheral stimulation, and cortical neuromodulation with adaptive dosing rules, biomarker-informed stratification, and ecologically valid task environments. The key challenge is not merely combining modalities, but coordinating them so that stimulation timing, task difficulty, and assistance level jointly maximize active participation and use-dependent plasticity ref [76], ref [77].

subsections.section_title: Integrated Imaging-Stimulation Strategies and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Therapeutic Translation in Sensory and Pain Recovery
subsections.content:
Therapeutic translation beyond motor recovery is increasingly relevant for post-stroke sensory deficits and central pain, where imaging can identify preserved pathways and stimulation-responsive networks. In visual rehabilitation, a pilot study combining anodal tDCS over lesioned occipital cortex with vision restoration training in subacute stroke reported excellent tolerability and larger gains in perimetric sensitivity than standard compensatory training, supporting the feasibility of pairing neuromodulation with task-specific sensory retraining early after injury [1]. Earlier comparative case studies in chronic hemianopia similarly suggested that tDCS can potentiate visual field training, consistent with a residual-network model of recovery rather than a purely compensatory mechanism [3,4,5].

For post-stroke central pain, mechanistic translation has been more explicitly imaging-led. High-frequency M1 rTMS produced modest but sustained analgesic effects in a subset of patients, and responsiveness correlated with preservation of the ipsilesional superior thalamocortical tract on diffusion imaging and with reduced pain-network activity on fMRI, including secondary somatosensory, insular, prefrontal, putaminal, and cerebellar regions [2]. These findings align with earlier work showing that analgesic benefit from motor-cortex stimulation depends on pain origin and somatotopic targeting, and that tract integrity may constrain the propagation of stimulation effects across thalamocortical and sensorimotor circuits [6,7,8].

Clinically, these data argue for a more selective deployment of noninvasive stimulation in sensory and pain rehabilitation: stimulation should be coupled to active perceptual training when residual sensory representations are present, and guided by structural or functional markers of network preservation when treating central pain [1,2]. Future trials should therefore move beyond generic efficacy designs toward biomarker-stratified protocols, multimodal outcomes, and longer follow-up, while also accounting for affective state, which appears to modulate analgesic responsiveness after stroke [2,9,10].

subsections.section_title: Figures and Tabulated Summaries
subsections.subsection_title: Figures and Tabulated Summaries
subsections.content:
Figures in this review should synthesize the field along three axes: modality, rehabilitation target, and study design. A first overview figure can map how fMRI, EEG, fNIRS, and MEG capture complementary signatures of post-stroke motor reorganization, from large-scale network connectivity to oscillatory and hemodynamic task responses ref [72], ref [2], ref [7], ref [18]. A second figure can summarize stimulation paradigms—rTMS, tDCS, and multimodal stimulation-imaging combinations—by hemisphere targeted, excitation/inhibition principle, and expected mechanisms such as interhemispheric rebalance or ipsilesional facilitation ref [51], ref [62], ref [54].

Tabulated summaries are particularly valuable because evidence is heterogeneous in lesion location, chronicity, motor severity, stimulation dose, and outcome selection. A compact study table should therefore report cohort features, imaging/stimulation protocol, motor task, primary endpoints, and main neural findings, enabling readers to compare prognostic imaging studies with intervention studies in a common format ref [26], ref [28], ref [53]. Separate tables are also useful for concurrent or hybrid approaches, including EEG-fMRI, EEG-fNIRS, and neuroimaging-guided stimulation, where acquisition feasibility and interpretability are central to translational value ref [41], ref [71].

For maximal utility, figures and tables should emphasize patterns rather than cataloging studies alone: whether biomarkers are predictive versus mechanistic, whether stimulation effects are state-dependent, and which modalities are practical for bedside or longitudinal deployment. Such presentation helps clarify where evidence is strongest—e.g., network-level fMRI and electrophysiological markers for recovery tracking, and noninvasive stimulation protocols with meta-analytic support for upper-limb outcomes—while also revealing gaps in standardization and multimodal validation ref [72], ref [51], ref [54], ref [53].
